title: Daily Water Intake Calculator 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
description: Sports-nutritionist daily water intake calculator. Galpin protocol (0.5 oz/lb base + exercise + climate). NAM DRI, ACSM 2007 fluid replacement, sweat rate test.
seoKeywords: how much water should I drink
intro: Hydration is the single biggest performance lever most US athletes underestimate. Your daily water needs aren't 8 glasses — they're a moving target driven by body weight, training load, sweat rate, and climate. This calculator uses the NAM DRI baseline (3.7 L/day men, 2.7 L/day women), then layers Dr. Andy Galpin's practical protocol on top: 0.5 oz per pound of body weight as your floor, plus 12–16 oz per hour of training, plus a climate factor when ambient heat or humidity drive sweat losses above 1 L/h. The ACSM Position Stand on Exercise & Fluid Replacement (2007) recommends replacing 100% of sweat losses during sessions over 60 minutes, and adding 500–1000 mL when ambient temps exceed 85°F. Sweat rates vary wildly — from 0.5 L/h in a 70°F gym to 2.5 L/h in a summer marathon — so generic '8 cups' advice fails most active people. Use the inputs below for your personalized number in oz and liters, then run the sweat rate test in the explanation section to dial it in further.
keyTakeaway: Base hydration = 0.5 oz × body weight (lb) per day. Add 12–16 oz per hour of training. Add 500–1000 mL more when training above 85°F or at altitude. Replace 100% of sweat losses during exercise over 60 minutes.
useCases: Marathon and triathlon training through hot summer months (July–August US)

explanation:
Daily water needs are not 8 glasses. They depend on body mass, training load, sweat rate, and the climate you train in. As a sports nutritionist working with US athletes, here is how I actually program hydration.

## NAM DRI Baseline (Sedentary Floor)

The National Academies of Medicine (formerly IOM) Dietary Reference Intake for water sets the sedentary adult floor at **3.7 L/day for men and 2.7 L/day for women**, including water from food (roughly 20% of total intake). For a 180 lb male, that means about 3.0 L from beverages alone before any training. This is the floor — not the target for anyone exercising.

## Galpin Practical Protocol

Dr. Andy Galpin's protocol is the simplest workable rule for active people:

- **Base**: 0.5 oz × body weight in lb per day. A 180 lb athlete = 90 oz (~2.7 L).
- **Training**: add **12–16 oz per hour of training** (350–470 mL/h).
- **Climate**: add **500–1000 mL** extra when training above 85°F or in humid conditions where WBGT exceeds 28°C.
- **Altitude**: add **1–2 L** when above 5,000 ft due to increased ventilation and diuresis.

For a 180 lb runner doing a 90-minute long run in 90°F Florida summer: 90 oz base + 24 oz mid-run + 24 oz heat add = ~138 oz (4.1 L) for the day.

## ACSM Position Stand 2007 — Exercise & Fluid Replacement

The American College of Sports Medicine published the gold-standard protocol in Sawka et al., *Med Sci Sports Exerc* 2007:

- **Pre-exercise**: 5–7 mL/kg body weight, **4 hours before** the session. For a 75 kg athlete, that's 375–525 mL sipped over the morning.
- **Intra-exercise**: 0.4–0.8 L/h, matched to individual sweat rate. Practice this in training, not race day.
- **Post-exercise**: **1.5 L per kg lost** during the session. The extra 50% covers ongoing urinary losses during rehydration.

## The Sweat Rate Test (Do This)

Generic formulas only get you to ±30%. To know your real number:

1. Weigh yourself nude **before** a 1-hour training session.
2. Train at your typical intensity. Drink nothing.
3. Towel dry, weigh nude again immediately after.
4. **Weight loss in kg × 1.5 = liters you need per hour of similar training.**

A 75 kg cyclist who weighs 74 kg post-ride lost 1 kg → needs ~1.5 L/h on similar days. Repeat across temperatures (cool gym, hot outdoor) — your sweat rate is not constant.

## Electrolytes — When Plain Water Isn't Enough

Add electrolytes when training exceeds **60 minutes** or when sweat losses are high. Sodium is the priority because sweat sodium runs 200–2000 mg/L depending on the individual. Common US options per liter:

| Product | Sodium per L |
|---|---|
| Gatorade Endurance | 800 mg |
| LMNT | 1000 mg |
| Liquid IV | 500 mg |
| Skratch Sport | 380 mg |
| Nuun Sport | 300 mg |

For salty sweaters (visible white salt streaks on your kit), aim for 700–1000 mg sodium per liter. For low sweaters in cool conditions, 300–500 mg/L is plenty.

## Climate Adjustments

- **Hot >85°F**: add 500–1000 mL/day above baseline. Sweat rates can hit 2.0–2.5 L/h in marathoners.
- **Humid heat WBGT >32°C**: ACSM recommends cancelling outdoor exercise. Heat illness risk is non-linear.
- **Cold climates**: evaporative loss drops but you still lose 1–2 L/day through respiration (cold air is dry) and cold-induced diuresis. Don't under-drink in winter.
- **Altitude >5,000 ft**: hyperventilation and altitude diuresis drive an extra 1–2 L/day. Common mistake at ski resorts and altitude camps.

## Endurance Hyponatremia — The Real Risk

Over-drinking plain water during ultra-endurance events can cause **exercise-associated hyponatremia (EAH)**. Almond et al., *NEJM* 2005 found **13% of Boston Marathon finishers were hyponatremic** (Na <135 mmol/L), and 0.6% severely (Na <120). Risk factors: events >4 hours, low body mass, slow finish times, and drinking on a fixed schedule regardless of thirst. The fix: drink to thirst, include sodium when training >2 hours, and never out-drink your sweat rate. Casa et al., *Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab* 2013 also showed female athletes have lower sweat rates and slower gastric emptying, so the same fluid plan that works for a male training partner can overload a female athlete.

## Practice Your Race Plan

Don't try a new hydration protocol on race day. Gastric tolerance for fluid intake is trainable — practice your target intra-exercise rate during long training sessions. If you struggle with 0.8 L/h in training, you will not magically tolerate it in a marathon.

*Last reviewed: 2026-05-28.*

faq.q: How much water should I drink during a 1-hour workout?
faq.a: ACSM recommends 0.4–0.8 L/h (about 13–27 oz) during exercise, matched to your individual sweat rate. For most US athletes in moderate conditions, 16–20 oz of fluid spread across the hour is the sweet spot. Add electrolytes if the session exceeds 60 minutes or temps are high.

faq.q: How do I run the sweat rate test?
faq.a: Weigh yourself nude before a 1-hour training session. Train at typical intensity without drinking. Towel dry and weigh nude immediately after. Multiply weight loss in kg by 1.5 to get liters needed per hour of similar training. Repeat across temperatures because your sweat rate is not constant.

faq.q: Plain water vs sports drink — which one?
faq.a: Under 60 minutes of training in moderate temps, plain water is fine. Over 60 minutes or in heat above 85°F, add electrolytes — sodium 300–700 mg/L for most athletes, up to 1000 mg/L for salty sweaters. Gatorade Endurance, LMNT, and Liquid IV are common US options at different sodium concentrations.

faq.q: How much water do I need for hot yoga or Bikram?
faq.a: Hot yoga rooms run 90–105°F and sweat losses commonly hit 1.5–2.0 L per 90-minute class. Pre-hydrate with 16–20 oz two hours before, sip 8–12 oz during, and replace 1.5 L per kg lost afterward with sodium added — plain water alone post-class is a hyponatremia risk.

faq.q: Do I really need less water in cold climates?
faq.a: No. Evaporative sweat loss drops in winter, but you still lose 1–2 L/day through respiration (cold air is extremely dry) and cold-induced diuresis. Most US athletes under-drink in winter because thirst is suppressed in the cold. Stick close to your warm-weather baseline minus 500 mL — not minus 2 L.

Yes, significantly. Above 5,000 ft, hyperventilation and altitude diuresis drive an extra 1–2 L/day of fluid loss. Skiers in Colorado, hikers in Utah, and athletes at altitude camps consistently underestimate this. Add 1 L for elevations 5,000–8,000 ft and 2 L above 8,000 ft to your normal protocol.

faq.q: How do I avoid hyponatremia during a marathon or ultra?
faq.a: Almond et al. (NEJM 2005) found 13% of Boston Marathon finishers were hyponatremic. The fix: don't drink on a fixed schedule beyond your sweat rate. Cap intake at your tested sweat rate, include sodium (700–1000 mg/L) for events over 2 hours, and avoid drinking aggressively in the last hour. Thirst is a reasonable guide for trained endurance athletes.

faq.q: When should I start drinking before a workout?
faq.a: ACSM pre-exercise protocol: 5–7 mL per kg body weight, 4 hours before. A 75 kg (165 lb) athlete = 375–525 mL (13–18 oz) sipped over the morning. If urine is still dark 2 hours out, add another 3–5 mL/kg. Chugging water 15 minutes before just creates a sloshing stomach during the warmup.

faq.q: Do women need a different hydration protocol than men?
faq.a: Yes. Casa et al. (Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab 2013) found female athletes have lower average sweat rates and slower gastric emptying. The same intra-exercise fluid plan that works for a male training partner can overload a female athlete. Run your own sweat rate test rather than copying a partner's protocol — sex-based averages are starting points, not prescriptions.
